column4: At the inheritance division (ٱلْقِسْمَةَ), relatives, orphans, and the needy are present and the command فَٱرْزُقُوهُم مِّنْهُ gives them provision from it, assembling the section's whole table in one act.
وَلَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ repeats the section's failure to urge feeding the needy; its singular verb also clarifies what the reciprocal plural in 89:18 makes a communal failure.
وَلَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ is the same refused urging, now named as a cause of the left-hand recipient's punishment.
نَصِيبًۭا مَّفْرُوضًۭا makes inheritance an obligatory apportioned share for women as well as men, the precise boundary erased when the legacy is eaten all together.
The ban on eating orphan property by adding it إِلَىٰٓ أَمْوَٰلِكُمْ directly opposes the section's لَمًّا, which gathers distinguishable shares into one mass.

Those who eat orphan wealth unjustly إِنَّمَا يَأْكُلُونَ فِى بُطُونِهِمْ نَارًۭا makes literal the section's meeting between devouring the weak person's property and the fire the eater finally meets.
نَحْنُ قَسَمْنَا بَيْنَهُم مَّعِيشَتَهُمْ states that God, rather than the hoarder, apportions livelihoods; the q-s-m root joins the oath-word to the division of life's means.
ٱللَّهُ يَبْسُطُ ٱلرِّزْقَ ... وَيَقْدِرُ directly supplies the section's claim that provision is expanded or measured narrowly by God, while the verse relativizes worldly enjoyment.
مَن قُدِرَ عَلَيْهِ رِزْقُهُ closely repeats 89:16, but commands the person under that constraint to spend from what God gave and promises ease after hardship.
وَإِنَّهُۥ لِحُبِّ ٱلْخَيْرِ لَشَدِيدٌ is the Quran's other concentrated portrait of intense love of wealth, directly echoing حُبًّا جَمًّا.
ٱلَّذِى جَمَعَ مَالًۭا وَعَدَّدَهُۥ stages the section's full vessel as a person gathering wealth and repeatedly counting it.
The collector يَحْسَبُ أَنَّ مَالَهُۥٓ أَخْلَدَهُۥ mistakes accumulated wealth for permanence, exposing the hope hidden inside the filled jar.
وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعَىٰٓ shows the same two motions as the section's image: gathering and putting the result into a containing vessel.
أَوْ إِطْعَٰمٌۭ فِى يَوْمٍۢ ذِى مَسْغَبَةٍۢ makes feeding on a day of hunger the concrete crossing of the steep path.
يَتِيمًۭا ذَا مَقْرَبَةٍ identifies the near orphan as one recipient of the feeding in 90:14, joining kinship and orphanhood at the table.
أَوْ مِسْكِينًۭا ذَا مَتْرَبَةٍۢ identifies the other recipient as a needy person brought down to the dust, making the section's dictionary sense of weakness visible.
The left-hand recipient's مَآ أَغْنَىٰ عَنِّى مَالِيَهْ declares the final uselessness of the wealth whose gathering displaced the needy; 69:25 identifies the speaker.
Hell is addressed as a vessel, هَلِ ٱمْتَلَأْتِ, and answers هَلْ مِن مَّزِيدٍۢ; it is the terrible, never-satisfied endpoint of the nearly overflowing wealth-container.
أَلْهَىٰكُمُ ٱلتَّكَاثُرُ names the rivalry in increase that the section hears in the old sense of 89:12's multiplying verb.
إِنَّا نَحْنُ نَرِثُ ٱلْأَرْضَ وَمَنْ عَلَيْهَا states the final transfer: God remains, inherits earth and everyone on it, and all return to Him.

The question why people do not spend is grounded in وَلِلَّهِ مِيرَٰثُ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ, so divine inheritance turns the section's claim about ultimate ownership into a demand to release wealth now.
Those who clutch God's bounty will have it collared around them, while وَلِلَّهِ مِيرَٰثُ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ denies that their hoard was ever finally theirs.
Fay is assigned to kin, orphans, the needy, and the traveler كَىْ لَا يَكُونَ دُولَةًۢ بَيْنَ ٱلْأَغْنِيَآءِ, an explicit rule against wealth circulating only at the rich end of the table.
The fifth of spoils is apportioned to God, the Messenger, kin, orphans, the needy, and the traveler, directly realizing the dictionary sense of dividing booty among its proper recipients.

Property is called the means God made قِيَٰمًۭا, and guardians must وَٱرْزُقُوهُمْ فِيهَا; this directly supports the section's claim that a vulnerable person's provision lets that person remain standing.
Guardians must hand orphans their property and not eat it wastefully or hastily before they grow, a precise procedural barrier against consuming the whole legacy.
The prescribed shares for children and parents enact the separation of an inheritance into its owners' portions rather than allowing an undivided eater to seize it.
The spouses' and siblings' shares continue the measured inheritance table, repeatedly calling each allocation فَرِيضَةًۭ مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ.
The ruling concerns orphan women whose prescribed due is withheld and weak children, then commands justice for orphans; it directly exposes who is erased when inheritance is swallowed whole.
The final inheritance ruling assigns the kalalah estate by stated fractions, reinforcing that a legacy passes by measured shares rather than indiscriminate gathering.
لَا تَأْكُلُوٓا۟ أَمْوَٰلَكُم بَيْنَكُم بِٱلْبَٰطِلِ generalizes the section's eating image to all wrongful appropriation of one another's property.
The command not to eat one another's wealth unjustly or use rulers to consume a portion of others' property gives the legal-social form of the section's predatory eating.
Religious authorities يَأْكُلُونَ أَمْوَٰلَ ٱلنَّاسِ بِٱلْبَٰطِلِ while others hoard gold and silver instead of spending, joining wrongful eating and the filled hoard in one verse.
The hoard from 9:34 is heated in Hell and brands foreheads, sides, and backs, making stored wealth itself the fire with which its keepers meet.
وَفِىٓ أَمْوَٰلِهِمْ حَقٌّۭ لِّلسَّآئِلِ وَٱلْمَحْرُومِ places a due share for the asker and deprived inside the owner's wealth, exactly the portion the section says must leave the vessel.
The prayerful have حَقٌّۭ مَّعْلُومٌۭ in their wealth, a known and measured share opposed to indiscriminate accumulation.
لِّلسَّآئِلِ وَٱلْمَحْرُومِ names the requester and deprived as owners of the known share in 70:24.
When told to spend from God's provision, disbelievers ask whether they should feed one whom God could feed; the objection directly dramatizes a community refusing to turn apportioned rizq into food.
وَلَمْ نَكُ نُطْعِمُ ٱلْمِسْكِينَ is the condemned speakers' own admission that they did not feed the needy, one stated cause of entering Saqar.
فَذَٰلِكَ ٱلَّذِى يَدُعُّ ٱلْيَتِيمَ supplies the orphan-repelling act paired with refusal to urge needy-food in 107:3.
أُوتِىَ كِتَٰبَهُۥ بِشِمَالِهِ identifies the left-hand recipient whose useless wealth, chaining, and failure to urge feeding unfold in 69:28-37.
خُذُوهُ فَغُلُّوهُ begins the chaining whose causes are separately named in 69:33-34, giving the section's claimed consequence its own action.
ثُمَّ ٱلْجَحِيمَ صَلُّوهُ moves the one who withheld food and gathered wealth into the fire, completing the devouring-to-fire trajectory.
The command to thread him through a seventy-cubit chain specifies the binding that the section says follows the refused urging of needy-food.
Failure to believe in God is named as the first cause beside failure to urge feeding in 69:34, preserving the passage's two stated grounds rather than making food the sole cause.
وَلَا طَعَامٌ إِلَّا مِنْ غِسْلِينٍ reverses the withheld table: the one who did not urge feeding now has no food except foul discharge.
لَّا يَأْكُلُهُۥٓ إِلَّا ٱلْخَٰطِـُٔونَ identifies the sinners as eaters of that hellish food, closing the reversal begun by eating others' shares.
فَلَا ٱقْتَحَمَ ٱلْعَقَبَةَ frames the feeding acts of 90:14-16 as the difficult moral ascent the hoarder has declined.
فَكُّ رَقَبَةٍۢ places freeing a person alongside hungry-day feeding, widening the steep path from food to release of the vulnerable.
Mutual counsel to patience and mercy gives a positive communal counterpart to the reciprocal urging abandoned in 89:18.
Spending wealth is pictured as one حَبَّةٍۢ growing seven ears of a hundred grains: the section's grain-sense of h-b-b leaves the hoard and becomes true increase through giving.
If God expanded provision without limit people would transgress, so He sends it down بِقَدَرٍۢ مَّا يَشَآءُ; measured provision is presented as protection from the excess seen in the filled vessel.
Every thing has its treasuries with God, but He sends it down only بِقَدَرٍۢ مَّعْلُومٍۢ, joining stored abundance to an exact released measure.
قَدْ جَعَلَ ٱللَّهُ لِكُلِّ شَىْءٍۢ قَدْرًۭا states almost verbatim the section's dictionary premise that every thing has a measure.
وَقَدَّرَ فِيهَآ أَقْوَٰتَهَا apportions the earth's sustenance in measured stages, equally for those who ask, uniting measure, food-support, and claimants.
God has favored some in provision, yet the favored refuse to return their provision to those under their authority so that they might share equally; unequal rizq becomes a test of withheld sharing.
The one granted good provision فَهُوَ يُنفِقُ مِنْهُ سِرًّۭا وَجَهْرًا spends from it secretly and openly, the opposite motion from filling and sealing the vessel.
إِنَّ رَبَّكَ يَبْسُطُ ٱلرِّزْقَ ... وَيَقْدِرُ repeats the exact divine expansion and restriction that governs the section's idea of each person's measured share.
After Qarun's collapse, those who desired his place recognize that God expands and restricts provision; the scene corrects the reading of abundant wealth as honor.
ٱللَّهُ يَبْسُطُ ٱلرِّزْقَ ... وَيَقْدِرُ لَهُ repeats the apportioning formula and grounds it in God's knowledge of all things.
The question whether they see God expand and restrict provision makes changing allotment itself a sign, rather than proof of a person's worth.
The answer to those boasting of greater wealth and children is that God expands and restricts provision, but most do not know what that abundance means.
After repeating expansion and restriction, the verse promises وَمَآ أَنفَقْتُم مِّن شَىْءٍۢ فَهُوَ يُخْلِفُهُۥ, turning divinely apportioned provision into confidence to spend.
The verse again asks whether people know that God expands and restricts provision, making the measure a sign against self-credit for wealth.
God holds the keys of heaven and earth and expands or restricts provision, locating every human vessel inside His larger store and measure.
The answer to what should be spent names parents, kin, orphans, the needy, and the traveler, directing wealth toward almost the same absent guests as the section's table.
Obligatory alms are expressly apportioned among the poor, needy, collectors, reconciliation, freeing people, debtors, God's way, and travelers, a divinely fixed counter-table to private accumulation.
وَءَاتِ ذَا ٱلْقُرْبَىٰ حَقَّهُۥ وَٱلْمِسْكِينَ commands delivery of the relative's due and the needy person's due, treating what leaves one's hand as their right.
فَـَٔاتِ ذَا ٱلْقُرْبَىٰ حَقَّهُۥ وَٱلْمِسْكِينَ again calls the portion given to relatives and the needy their due, not the owner's optional surplus.
People of wealth and abundance are forbidden to swear off giving kin, the needy, and emigrants, directly addressing the full vessel's temptation to close itself.
ٱسْتَطْعَمَآ أَهْلَهَا stages the dictionary form cited in the section: two travelers ask a town for food, and its people refuse them hospitality.
فِدْيَةٌۭ طَعَامُ مِسْكِينٍۢ makes feeding a needy person the concrete compensatory act for one unable to fast.
The expiation feeds ten needy people from the average food used for one's own family, bringing the poor onto the same standard of table rather than assigning scraps.
Feeding sixty needy people is the required expiation for one unable to perform the preceding remedies, another legal scene in which food becomes the needy person's due.
At harvest, وَءَاتُوا۟ حَقَّهُۥ يَوْمَ حَصَادِهِۦ commands release of the crop's due and immediately forbids excess, joining grain, entitlement, and the boundary on filling oneself.
وَيْلٌۭ لِّلْمُطَفِّفِينَ condemns those who manipulate the measure, the commercial form of taking more than one's apportioned share.
When they take measure from people, يَسْتَوْفُونَ, they demand it in full, showing the vessel filled at the powerful person's end.
When measuring or weighing for others, they diminish, making the needy end of the same transaction underfilled.
أَوْفُوا۟ ٱلْكَيْلَ commands a full measure while forbidding those who cause loss, establishing the just boundary for the section's brimful measuring vessel.
وَزِنُوا۟ بِٱلْقِسْطَاسِ ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمِ adds the straight balance to the command for full measure.
Do not diminish people's things or spread corruption in the land; it connects unjust measure to the same corruption whose multiplication the section hears in 89:12.
Shuayb's command combines full measure and weight, refusal to deprive people of their things, and refusal to corrupt the earth, the whole ethical boundary around the filled container.
Shuayb sees his people in prosperity yet fears punishment while forbidding deficient measure and weight, showing abundance does not authorize taking another's share.
The command to fulfill measure and weight justly and not diminish people's goods directly regulates how a provisioned community portions its table.
The she-camel trial declares that water is قِسْمَةٌۢ بَيْنَهُمْ and each drinking turn is attended, a concrete instance of one gathered resource becoming scheduled shares.
People assign God a share of crops and cattle, then let the partners' portion displace God's; the corrupt partition of provision exposes how a declared share can be redirected by power.
They assign to unknown objects نَصِيبًۭا مِّمَّا رَزَقْنَٰهُمْ, joining provision and portion in a wrongful distribution for which they will be questioned.
Qarun is told to seek the Hereafter through what God gave, not forget his worldly share, do good, and not seek corruption; it sets apportioned use against hoarded, corrupting abundance.
أَن لَّا يَدْخُلَنَّهَا ٱلْيَوْمَ عَلَيْكُم مِّسْكِينٌۭ is the garden owners' whispered plan to exclude every needy person from the harvest.
The fertile garden becomes كَٱلصَّرِيمِ overnight, an emptied field answering the owners' determination to keep its full yield from the needy.
وَيُطْعِمُونَ ٱلطَّعَامَ عَلَىٰ حُبِّهِۦ gives beloved food to the needy, orphan, and captive; the same love that fills 89's vessel here empties it into other mouths.
Righteousness includes giving wealth عَلَىٰ حُبِّهِۦ to kin, orphans, the needy, traveler, requester, and for liberation, reversing love of wealth into a shared table.
لَن تَنَالُوا۟ ٱلْبِرَّ حَتَّىٰ تُنفِقُوا۟ مِمَّا تُحِبُّونَ makes spending precisely what one loves the road to goodness, rather than love's reason for retaining it.
The hosts prefer others over themselves وَلَوْ كَانَ بِهِمْ خَصَاصَةٌۭ, even in need, and are saved from avarice; their vessel opens despite its own shortfall.
فَأَمَّا مَنْ أَعْطَىٰ وَٱتَّقَىٰ begins the opposite type from the self-sufficient miser: the person who gives and remains mindful.
Believing in the best promise gives the giver's release of wealth its inward ground.
فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُۥ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ promises ease to the giver, reversing the instinct that safety comes from keeping the vessel full.
The person who withholds and deems himself self-sufficient embodies the closed, full vessel.
فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُۥ لِلْعُسْرَىٰ answers the withholder's imagined security with a course toward hardship.
وَمَا يُغْنِى عَنْهُۥ مَالُهُۥٓ إِذَا تَرَدَّىٰ repeats the left-hand recipient's discovery that amassed wealth cannot avail at the fall.
Usurious increase does not grow with God, whereas what is given as zakat seeking Him makes its givers the true multipliers; it reverses the section's worldly contest in increase.
مَا عِندَكُمْ يَنفَدُ وَمَا عِندَ ٱللَّهِ بَاقٍۢ distinguishes the exhaustible contents people hold from what remains with God, exposing the false permanence of accumulation.
Wealth and children are the adornment of the near life, while enduring good deeds are better in reward and hope; the verse separates the filled vessel from what actually lasts.
Worldly life includes boasting and تَكَاثُرٌۭ فِى ٱلْأَمْوَٰلِ, then becomes dry debris like rain-grown plants, making the contest in increase visibly perishable.
Believers are warned not to let wealth and children distract them from remembrance, matching the distraction named by ٱلتَّكَاثُرُ while marking its remedy.
Spend from provision before death, when the withholder will ask for delay to give charity; the sealed vessel is opened only too late.
Those called to spend yet act stingily are stingy only against themselves; God is rich and they are poor, reversing the hoarder's estimate of who possesses and who needs.
The wealth-counter is hurled into ٱلْحُطَمَةِ, so the container he filled does not preserve him but leads to crushing destruction.
نَارُ ٱللَّهِ ٱلْمُوقَدَةُ identifies the Crusher as God's kindled fire, completing the section's turn from gathered wealth to consuming flame.
The fire following the stower's refusal is لَظَىٰ, introducing the consuming answer to gathering and putting away in 70:18.
The blaze تَدْعُوا۟ مَنْ أَدْبَرَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ calls the person who turned away before 70:18 names his gathering and storage.
حَتَّىٰ زُرْتُمُ ٱلْمَقَابِرَ gives the contest for more its limit in the grave, where no filled store remains usable.
لَتَرَوُنَّ ٱلْجَحِيمَ shows the fire at the end of the rivalry for increase announced in 102:1.
ثُمَّ لَتُسْـَٔلُنَّ يَوْمَئِذٍ عَنِ ٱلنَّعِيمِ turns enjoyed abundance into a questioned trust rather than proof of honor.
مَآ أَغْنَىٰ عَنْهُ مَالُهُۥ وَمَا كَسَبَ repeats the verdict that wealth and acquisition do not avail their owner.
سَيَصْلَىٰ نَارًۭا ذَاتَ لَهَبٍۢ places the owner whose wealth does not avail directly into flame.
يَوْمَ لَا يَنفَعُ مَالٌۭ وَلَا بَنُونَ states the final boundary at which wealth and children provide no benefit.
The disbelievers' wealth and children will avail nothing, and they become وَقُودُ ٱلنَّارِ; stored assets fail while their owners become fuel.
Even مِلْءُ ٱلْأَرْضِ ذَهَبًۭا, an earth-full quantity of gold, cannot ransom the one who dies rejecting faith, giving the full-container image its absolute limit.
Whatever people are given is temporary worldly enjoyment and adornment, while what is with God is better and lasting, separating a present share from permanent possession.
Whatever is given is merely enjoyment of the near life, while what is with God is better and more lasting for those who trust Him.
لَأَمْلَأَنَّ جَهَنَّمَ مِنكُمْ أَجْمَعِينَ sets a decreed filling of Hell beside 50:30's still-demanding vessel; together they mark how different this fullness is from sufficiency.
لَأَمْلَأَنَّ جَهَنَّمَ مِنَ ٱلْجِنَّةِ وَٱلنَّاسِ أَجْمَعِينَ repeats the decree to fill Hell, sharpening the paradox of the vessel that in 50:30 asks for more.
The promise to fill Hell with jinn and humans gives a fixed divine boundary to the otherwise insatiable image of 50:30.
لَأَمْلَأَنَّ جَهَنَّمَ مِنكَ وَمِمَّن تَبِعَكَ closes the series of filling decrees and locates what the terrible vessel will contain.
After the measured inheritance shares, obedience to those limits leads to gardens; this is the positive boundary around the division.
Transgressing the inheritance limits leads to abiding fire, joining violation of apportioned shares to the section's fiery endpoint.
A visitation from the Lord circles the garden while its owners sleep, beginning the loss that answers their plan to reserve every share.
بَلْ نَحْنُ مَحْرُومُونَ makes the would-be deprivers recognize themselves as the deprived after the crop is taken away.
The owners confess إِنَّا كُنَّا طَٰغِينَ, naming exclusion of the needy from abundance as transgression.
The earth swallows Qarun and his house, and no faction or self-help can preserve the amassed abundance.
The love of desires is adorned, including heaped gold and silver; its قَنَٰطِيرِ ٱلْمُقَنطَرَةِ gives the section's intense love of wealth an explicitly piled material form.
إِنَّمَآ أَمْوَٰلُكُمْ وَأَوْلَٰدُكُمْ فِتْنَةٌ identifies wealth as a trial, supporting the section's correction of the claim that expanded or restricted provision proves honor or humiliation.
The command to spend and the promise of success for one protected from inner stinginess show how the wealth-trial in 64:15 is passed.
The command to worship God is immediately joined to good treatment of parents, kin, orphans, the needy, neighbors, travelers, and dependents, laying out the social table around property.
The condemned are stingy, command other people to stinginess, and hide God's bounty; this is the communal reverse of urging one another toward feeding.
فَأَمَّا ٱلْيَتِيمَ فَلَا تَقْهَرْ forbids overpowering the orphan, the vulnerable heir standing beside the needy in the section.
وَأَمَّا ٱلسَّآئِلَ فَلَا تَنْهَرْ forbids repelling the requester, making visible the person who asks the full vessel for food.
The sacrificial provision is to be eaten and shared with ٱلْبَآئِسَ ٱلْفَقِيرَ, placing the afflicted poor at a communal meal.
From the sacrificial animals, people are told to eat and feed both the contented and the one who asks, another table whose provision must circulate.
Spend from what God provided before a day without trade or rescuing friendship; apportioned provision has a time in which it can still be released.
Spend from the good things earned and produced from earth, and do not select what is defective for others; the shared table must receive food the giver would accept.
The restrained poor are mistaken for self-sufficient because they do not ask insistently, showing that the needy person's absent request does not erase the share within the full vessel.
Many creatures do not carry their provision; God provides them and people alike, loosening the imagined security of a personally stocked container.
The question who could provide if God withheld His provision exposes every stored share as dependent on continued divine giving.
وَفِى ٱلسَّمَآءِ رِزْقُكُمْ locates people's provision beyond the vessel they presently control, reinforcing that its source and promised measure are not theirs.
لَا نَسْـَٔلُكَ رِزْقًۭا نَّحْنُ نَرْزُقُكَ reverses the direction of dependence: God asks no provision from the household but provides it.
Abraham settles his offspring in an uncultivated valley and asks that they be provided with fruits; provision is what enables dwelling in the section's secondary s-k-n sense.
A secure, settled town receives abundant provision from every place, then ingratitude turns that abundance into enveloping hunger and fear.
Towns made insolent by livelihood become dwellings scarcely inhabited, and وَكُنَّا نَحْنُ ٱلْوَٰرِثِينَ joins lost sustenance, lost dwelling, and God's final inheritance.
Every creature's provision rests with God, who knows its dwelling place and repository; the verse explicitly holds rizq, staying, and storage together.
Joseph says أَنَا۠ أُوفِى ٱلْكَيْلَ while distributing grain and conditions the visitors' next ration, staging provision as a full, governed measure.
Without the brother, فَلَا كَيْلَ لَكُمْ عِندِى: the measured share can be withheld entirely, showing the authority embedded in control of the granary.
The distressed family brings scant merchandise and asks Joseph فَأَوْفِ لَنَا ٱلْكَيْلَ وَتَصَدَّقْ عَلَيْنَآ, linking full measure with generosity to people in need.
أَوْفُوا۟ ٱلْكَيْلَ إِذَا كِلْتُمْ commands fullness in measuring for another and an upright balance, a just use of the brimful measure.
Protection of orphan property stands in the same verse as full measure and weight with justice, joining the vulnerable owner to honest apportionment.
God sets the balance after raising heaven, placing human measures under a larger created order.
أَلَّا تَطْغَوْا۟ فِى ٱلْمِيزَانِ forbids excess in the balance, the boundary violated by taking more than one's share.
Establish weight with justice and do not make the balance deficient; both overfilling oneself and underfilling another are corrected.
فَلْيَنظُرِ ٱلْإِنسَٰنُ إِلَىٰ طَعَامِهِۦ asks the human to look at the origin of his food before the passage names the grain.
فَأَنۢبَتْنَا فِيهَا حَبًّۭا gives the Quranic grain-sense of h-b-b cited by the section and locates the desired food in God's growth from earth.
مَّتَٰعًۭا لَّكُمْ وَلِأَنْعَٰمِكُمْ names the whole food-producing sequence as provision for people and their animals.
From dead earth God brings out حَبًّۭا فَمِنْهُ يَأْكُلُونَ, directly joining the section's grain-sense of h-b-b to eating.
Blessed water descends and grows gardens and grain, supplying the water-mass and grain inside the section's imagined full jar from one divine source.
Tall palms with clustered spathes add a visibly gathered, layered crop to the provision scene.
رِّزْقًۭا لِّلْعِبَادِ names the rain-grown grain and fruit as provision for servants, rather than the accumulator's self-created stock.
The owners of the garden swear to harvest it in the morning, opening a scene of abundant food treated as exclusively theirs.
They make no exception, showing confidence that the crop and its measure are fully under their control.
They set out early to cut the crop, moving toward the act that would fill their own containers.
They go out عَلَىٰ حَرْدٍۢ قَٰدِرِينَ with determined confidence in their power, while the garden has already been emptied beyond their knowledge.
Their most balanced member asks why they did not glorify God, identifying forgotten divine ownership inside the failed harvest plan.
After losing the crop, they hope their Lord will exchange it for a better garden, turning ownership back into dependence on divine allotment.
كَذَٰلِكَ ٱلْعَذَابُ makes the emptied garden an anticipatory judgment and points beyond it to the greater final punishment.
Qarun's treasure-keys burden a strong company, and his people tell him not to exult; the full vessel has become physically and morally heavy.
Qarun attributes the wealth to knowledge he possesses, precisely the self-credit corrected when survivors recognize divine expansion and restriction in 28:82.
Qarun comes out in adornment and people desiring worldly life wish for wealth like his, showing the social contagion of the competition for more.
Those given knowledge answer that God's reward is better, providing the interpretive boundary before Qarun and his store disappear.
The garden owner boasts أَنَا۠ أَكْثَرُ مِنكَ مَالًۭا and greater manpower, a narrative embodiment of rivalry in abundance.
Entering his garden while wronging himself, he says it will never perish, joining fullness to the fantasy of permanence.
He doubts the Hour and expects an even better return, extending wealth's false promise beyond death.
When the fruit is destroyed, he turns his palms over what he spent while the garden lies ruined, the full estate abruptly emptied.
No company can help him apart from God and he cannot help himself, exposing the social power attached to abundance as unusable.
A rejecter claims he will surely be given wealth and children, carrying the assumption that possession is a continuing personal entitlement.
وَنَرِثُهُۥ مَا يَقُولُ strips that claimant of the wealth he names and makes God its inheritor while he comes alone.
كَذَٰلِكَ وَأَوْرَثْنَٰهَا قَوْمًا ءَاخَرِينَ is the section's dictionary definition of inheritance staged historically: one people's goods become another people's possession.
وَأَوْرَثْنَٰهَا بَنِىٓ إِسْرَٰٓءِيلَ names the recipients when Pharaoh's people leave gardens, springs, treasures, and honored dwellings.
God causes the believers to inherit enemies' land, houses, and wealth, another collective transfer illustrating the section's basic w-r-th sense.
The oppressed people inherit the blessed eastern and western lands, reversing possession from oppressors to the formerly weak.
